children: Latin America and the Caribbean could add more than 5% to the region's economic output within a decade with broad adoption of artificial intelligence, although it will require governments to implement the right policies, the Inter-American Development Bank said in a report.

Latin America and the Caribbean has suffered for decades from low productivity. Gross domestic product per capita has been around a quarter of what it is in the U.S. since 1960, the IDB said Monday in its latest Development in the Americas report.
Broad adoption of AI could boost GDP in the region by as much as 5.1% after 10 years, and wages could increase by 4.2% in the same period, the bank said.

Use of AI can increase growth by raising productivity of workers and machines, as well as accelerating innovation, said Julián Cristia, a principal economist in the bank's research department and a co-editor of the report.
"But if the adoption is slow, and the productivity benefits are small, then this boost in growth could be only 0.3%," he said.

The private sector has a critical role to play in this process through innovation and adoption, while governments need to create the right regulatory environment and infrastructure, and to develop the necessary skills, he said.
Higher levels of education correspond with greater use of AI, he added.

Digital foundations in the region are insufficient with 83% of adults using the internet compared with 93% in countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, the IDB said. Only 26% of adults report having recently interacted with government digitally, compared with 70% in OECD countries.
The region is also running behind developed economies in adopting AI. In 2025-26, 35% of adults reported using generative AI compared with 43% in European OECD countries and 58% in the U.S.

"Although many organizations are experimenting with AI, smaller and informal firms often lack the managerial capabilities, financing and technological support needed to adopt it effectively," the bank said.
The model used by the IBD in its report was based on existing AI tools and capabilities, so advances over the next decade could add to potential growth, Cristia said.

AI technologies also carry risks that need to be managed, such as the impact on labor markets, cyber threats and privacy breaches, he said. "We will need to change how we work, but also there are going to be people that will transition to jobs that are expanding or occupations that are going to be new."

There is also risk of worker displacement with the adoption of AI, where workers with higher levels of education who perform cognitive talks are more exposed, according to the report. "Some workers with lower levels of education may gain because they face lower displacement risk and benefit from the demand expansion that accompanies higher output."
Formal workers are more directly exposed to displacement than informal workers, and high levels of informality in the region will limit gains from AI, the report said.
